chapter: Jimmy Butts, Doc Pittman and women in jazz
title: The Cajun Restaurant jazz brunch with Jimmy Butts and Doc Pittman
summary: She played a Sunday jazz brunch quintet from 1990 to 2005 led by Jimmy Butts with Doc Pittman, who taught her showmanship and professional demeanor.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: Are there places in town where people still dance to jazz music?

Oh yeah, yeah, well big band jazz most times, yeah there is. Like Red Blazer too I think it’s called Swing 46 now. Yeah. Swing 46. And there’s a few other places. And then in other cities you get those, it’s very nice. So yeah I mean I was lucky. I played at a jazz brunch from like 1990 to 2005 with a quintet that was just amazing and it was always full. They had it every Sunday and they served New Orleans cuisine. And the leader was named Jimmy Butts — Jimmy “The Face” Butts. He was an old bass player that had worked as a journalist as well. He was like he wrote for the Amsterdam News, he was a comedian, he could dance and sing and he was a wonderful bass player who had played with lots of great people. And his associate, Doc Pittman, who played the cocktail drum, you know it’s a stand-up drum you play it —

With brushes, yeah. And they were great entertainers. And Doc, I don’t know how he even made it to the club he was so old, and sort of limped along, but he brought four outfits so that he could change four times, one for each set. A powder blue suit with hat and jewelry and then a red one and a white one. And we would have these routines going and I just learned so much about the business and my playing just grew so much. It was just amazing. And they were so, like like if I even leaned my elbow on the piano while I was on stage, Jimmy would say, “Get your elbow off the piano, what is that?” You know? Just, you know the proper demeanor and the proper entertainment, which goes back to our discussion about not just being a musician. Like if I came in in a dress, “Where are your nylon stockings?” I mean —
They weren’t afraid to point that out.
Absolutely. And once I got off the stage because I was dizzy and Doc screamed his head off at me.
I was dizzy or something. He said, “This is entertainment. You don’t — there’s no such thing as not feeling well I mean it just doesn’t happen.” And that’s the standard he

applied to himself. I mean that’s how he did it. You have to look him up. Jimmy Butts and Doc Pittman. I mean they were just amazing. And the way they would fight like an old couple or something and not speak to each other. And they were just amazing. So I got a lot of training there.
Things you can’t learn in college.

Oh definitely not. It was called The Cajun Restaurant. And I still have like some videos on those old cassettes — videocassettes, that we made. I mean Doc had his own language. He had his own vocabulary. He would say, “Well I dig your ground pads.” That meant he liked your shoes. And he would call everyone Jack when he was telling a tale. “That’s the way it goes, Jack.”
